## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Apply a decision framework for when to customize: when
  context engineering is sufficient, when fine-tuning
  (PEFT/LoRA) is warranted, and when distillation or on-
  prem deployment is the right answer.
- Reason about institutional-data fine-tuning under HIPAA,
  including BAA constraints, audit requirements, and the
  reproducibility implications of model versioning.
- Design adoption patterns for research-analytics teams that
  reflect the *cybernetic teammate* evidence: AI-augmented
  individuals matching team-without-AI baselines, and the
  organizational R&D pattern for surfacing useful
  workflows.
- Distinguish productive adoption patterns (latent
  expertise at the edge, expert-in-the-loop verification)
  from anti-patterns (centralized IT prescription, AI as
  uncritical replacement).

## Orientation

The decision to customize a model, whether that means
fine-tuning it on institutional data, distilling a smaller
model from a larger one, or deploying an open-weights model
on-prem, is expensive in setup and maintenance. The default
for most research-analytics teams should be context
engineering: use a frontier API, supply institutional
context per query through RAG and prompt scaffolding, and
let the model do the work. Customization pays off only in a
narrow set of cases, and those are worth identifying
explicitly.

The adoption side of the chapter is equally important.
Mollick's *Cybernetic Teammate* RCT
[@mollick_2025_cybernetic_teammate] found that AI-enabled
individuals matched the performance of unaugmented
two-person teams. That evidence points to a specific
adoption pattern that works: latent-expertise discovery at
the team-member level, knowledge-sharing across the team,
and gradual codification of useful patterns into team-level
conventions. The anti-pattern, centralized IT prescription
of when and how AI should be used, is documented to
underperform.

The chapter develops three threads. **The customization
decision**: when context wins, when fine-tuning is
warranted, and when on-prem becomes necessary. **PEFT and
LoRA at a working level**: enough to make sound choices,
without going into the training mechanics that belong in a
different book. **Adoption patterns for research-analytics
teams**: how to organize the team's discovery and use of AI
assistance so the team's collective knowledge grows over
time.

## The researcher's contribution {#sec-customisation-teams-human}

Three judgments are not delegable.

**(Judgment 1.) The customization question is a
cost-benefit calculation, not an engineering preference.**
The temptation to fine-tune is strong. The customized model
feels like it is 'really yours'. The reality, however, is
that fine-tuning is expensive (in API cost, in
infrastructure, in maintenance) and obsoletes when the
underlying model is updated (which is often). Most
of the time, the right answer is context engineering
with a frontier API. The researcher evaluates the
trade rather than defaulting to one or the other.

**(Judgment 2.) Adoption is the longest-lived
artifact.** Specific models change every few months;
specific tools change every year. The team's
disposition toward AI-assisted work, the habits of
specification, verification, and disclosure, outlast
all of them. The researcher shapes the team's
adoption pattern with the long view in mind: build
habits that survive the next model release.

**(Judgment 3.) Centralized prescription does not
work.** The Mollick RCT and the *Latent Expertise*
[@mollick_2024_latent_expertise] argument both point in the
same direction: useful AI applications are
discovered by individual practitioners in their own
work, not prescribed by IT. The researcher's
role is to encourage individual experimentation,
share what works, and treat the discovery process as
part of the work. Trying to mandate specific tools
or prompts from above produces compliance theater
rather than productivity.

These judgments are what distinguish thoughtful
adoption from the patterns that produce expensive
failures (over-customized stacks, mandated tooling
that no one uses).

## Decision framework: when to customize

We find it helpful to picture the options as a ladder,
ordered from cheapest and least data-hungry at the
bottom to most expensive and most data-hungry at the
top: prompting, few-shot examples, RAG, parameter-
efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA), full fine-tuning,
and continued pretraining. @fig-customisation-ladder
renders the ladder as a decision tree. The rule for
climbing is the same at every rung: climb only when the
rung below demonstrably fails the team's evaluation
suite (@sec-evaluation), never because a higher rung
feels more thorough. Each step up multiplies cost and
the labeled data required, and most teams should stop
within the first two or three rungs.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-customisation-ladder
%%| fig-cap: "The customization ladder as a decision tree. Rungs are ordered by cost and by the volume of labeled data required, from prompting at the bottom to continued pretraining at the top. The gate at each rung is the same: climb only if the rung below fails the team's evaluation suite. Note that a shortfall of facts sends the researcher back to the retrieval corpus rather than up to a fine-tune, and that a full fine-tune is warranted only when a parameter-efficient adapter is insufficient and labeled data are plentiful."
flowchart TB
  S["Task with acceptance<br/>criteria and an eval suite"] --> R0{"Zero-shot prompting<br/>passes the eval suite?"}
  R0 -->|Yes| Stop["Stop. Do not climb.<br/>Higher rungs add cost,<br/>not quality."]
  R0 -->|No| R1{"Few-shot examples<br/>close the gap?"}
  R1 -->|Yes| Stop
  R1 -->|No| R2{"RAG over an<br/>institutional corpus<br/>closes the gap?"}
  R2 -->|Yes| Stop
  R2 -->|No| R3{"Is the gap in behaviour<br/>or style, not in<br/>missing facts?"}
  R3 -->|"No: facts are missing"| R2b["Improve the retrieval<br/>corpus, not the model"]
  R3 -->|"Yes: behaviour or style"| R4["PEFT: LoRA / QLoRA adapter<br/>1k to 10k labelled pairs"]
  R4 --> R5{"Adapter insufficient<br/>and labelled data<br/>plentiful?"}
  R5 -->|No| Stop
  R5 -->|Yes| R6["Full fine-tune<br/>10k to 100k+ pairs"]
  R6 --> R7{"Base lacks the domain's<br/>language entirely?"}
  R7 -->|No| Stop
  R7 -->|Yes| R8["Continued pretraining<br/>on a large domain corpus"]
```

A decision tree of this shape organizes the remaining
choice once the lower rungs are exhausted.

**Step 1: Is context engineering insufficient?**

Most tasks can be addressed by frontier-API + good
context (system prompt + retrieved documents +
structured input/output). If the model produces
acceptable results with this setup, do not customize.
Customisation pays off when context is genuinely
insufficient, not when it is annoying to set up.

Signs context engineering is sufficient:

- The frontier API produces correct output most of
  the time on the team's tasks.
- The remaining failures can be addressed by improved
  prompts or retrieval.
- The latency and cost are acceptable.

Signs context engineering is genuinely insufficient:

- The model consistently fails on tasks that require
  domain-specific terminology or conventions even
  with substantial context.
- The required context is so large it does not fit
  in the context window, or so complex that
  retrieval cannot reliably find the right pieces.
- Latency is unacceptable due to the size of context
  required per query.

**Step 2: If insufficient, what kind of customization?**

Three customization paths.

**Fine-tuning (PEFT / LoRA)** trains a small
adapter on top of a frontier model, leaving the base
model intact. The adapter encodes specific behaviors
(domain terminology, response style, structured-
output conventions) without retraining the base. PEFT
methods like LoRA [@hu_2022_lora] add a few million
parameters; QLoRA [@dettmers_2023_qlora] adds
quantization to make training feasible on modest
hardware. Cost: thousands of dollars in compute and
some weeks of work. Maintenance: the adapter needs
re-training when the base model is updated, which is
non-trivial.

**Distillation** trains a smaller model to mimic a
larger one on the team's tasks. The result is a
smaller, faster, cheaper model that performs well on
the specific tasks but does not have the larger
model's general capabilities. Useful when high-volume
inference cost is the binding constraint.

**On-prem open-weights deployment** runs an open-
weights model (BioMedLM [@bolton_2024_biomedlm], Llama
3, Mistral) on the institution's infrastructure. The
trade is operational: gain on-prem control of the
data and the model; lose the convenience of a managed
API. For PHI-heavy use cases where API
configuration is not adequate, this is the path.

**Step 3: Match path to use case.**

| Use case | Recommended path |
|----------|------------------|
| Domain-specific style or output format | LoRA fine-tune |
| High-volume inference at low latency | Distill to smaller model |
| Strict on-prem requirement (PHI, contractual) | Open-weights on-prem |
| Most everything else | Context engineering |

A common pattern: start with context engineering, observe
what specifically is failing, and customize narrowly to
address that. A blanket fine-tune of a frontier model
because 'we want our own model' is rarely the right
answer.

### A resource-constrained public-health example

To illustrate, consider a county health department with
a three-person analytics unit. Communicable-disease case
reports arrive as free-text clinician narratives, and the
unit must code each into a structured set of reportable-
condition categories for surveillance. The frontier-API
budget is small, the reports are PHI (so nothing leaves
the department's own infrastructure without a data-use
review), and the labeled set is thin: roughly 300
reports a prior analyst hand-coded. The unit weighs two
options: a RAG system that retrieves the case-definition
guidance and a few coded exemplars per query, or a LoRA
fine-tune on the 300 labeled reports.

The ladder in @fig-customisation-ladder settles it. RAG,
with few-shot prompting over the exemplars, sits below
LoRA on the ladder and demands no labeled training set,
only the case definitions and a handful of examples.
LoRA, by contrast, wants on the order of 1,000 to 10,000
labeled pairs (@tbl-customisation-methods), and 300 is
well short; an adapter trained on so few examples would
likely overfit to the prior analyst's idiosyncrasies
without generalizing. On the plus side, RAG keeps the
case definitions explicit and auditable, which matters
when a coding decision may later be questioned. On the
minus side, if the narratives lean on local abbreviations
and shorthand that no general model has seen, retrieval
of case definitions may not be enough, and the department
may find that a small QLoRA adapter, trainable on a
single on-prem GPU and keeping PHI in house
[@dettmers_2023_qlora], is warranted once it has labeled
enough reports to train on. The disciplined path is to
climb only when the rung below demonstrably fails: begin
with RAG plus few-shot, measure against a held-out set of
coded reports, and reserve the adapter for the gap that
remains. Should on-prem fine-tuning become necessary, a
model already pretrained on clinical text, such as
GatorTron [@yang_2022_gatortron], is the natural base,
since it has seen the register in which case reports are
written.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: when to fine-tune

**Question.** A research-analytics team has a frontier API
that produces acceptable results on most tasks but
fails on a specific kind of task: generating SAS code
in the institution's house style (specific macros,
indentation conventions, comment patterns). Should they
fine-tune?

**Answer.** Probably not yet. Try context engineering first: include
3–5 example outputs in the institution's house style as
part of the prompt or as a system-message example
library. Modern reasoning models pick up house style
from a few examples reliably. If that does not work
across enough variation, the next step is to build a
larger few-shot library with retrieval (the right
examples for the specific task). Only if that still
fails consistently, say, on novel tasks not represented
in the example library, does fine-tuning become worth
considering. The fine-tune cost ($1k–$5k in compute and
several weeks of work, plus maintenance when the base
model updates) is much higher than the example-library
cost.

:::

## PEFT, LoRA, and distillation at a working level

Three concepts at the level a researcher needs to
make sound choices.

**LoRA: low-rank adaptation.** Instead of fine-tuning all
parameters of a model, LoRA adds small low-rank
matrices to specific layers. The adapter has 0.1–1% as
many parameters as the base model. Training the
adapter is much cheaper than full fine-tuning and
empirically achieves similar performance on most tasks
[@hu_2022_lora].

The training process:

1. Collect training data, usually 1,000–10,000
   examples of input/output pairs in the desired
   style.
2. Set up a LoRA training environment (Hugging Face
   `peft` library is the reference).
3. Train the adapter for a small number of epochs
   (1–3 typically), monitoring loss on a held-out set.
4. Evaluate on a downstream task suite (the
   evaluation suite from @sec-evaluation).
5. If acceptable, deploy: the base model is loaded
   plus the adapter at inference time.

**QLoRA: quantized LoRA.** LoRA combined with 4-bit
quantization of the base model. Quantization reduces
memory requirements substantially, enabling LoRA
training on a single high-end GPU instead of a
multi-GPU cluster. The quality penalty is small for
most tasks. QLoRA is what makes LoRA training tractable
for individual research groups in 2026.

**Adapter management.** Multiple LoRA adapters can be
trained for the same base model, one for code
generation in the team's house style, another for
methods drafting in the team's voice, another for
RoB assessment. At inference, the appropriate adapter
is loaded for the task. Adapter swapping is cheaper
than maintaining multiple full models and is the
emerging pattern for organization-specific
customization.

**Maintenance.** When the base model is updated (a
new release of the same family, e.g., Llama 3.5 →
Llama 4), the adapter does not automatically
transfer. Re-training is required to get the
benefits of the base-model improvements while
preserving the customized behavior. This maintenance
overhead is the under-appreciated cost of fine-
tuning.

**Distillation** is conceptually different. A smaller
student model is trained to imitate a larger teacher
model's outputs on a target distribution of tasks.
The student is faster and cheaper at inference but
lacks the teacher's capability outside the trained
distribution.

For applied analytic work, distillation makes sense when:

- A specific repetitive task dominates inference cost
  (e.g., abstract screening for a living systematic
  review).
- The teacher model's capability on that task can
  be captured by the student.
- The deployment constraints favor the smaller
  model (latency, cost, on-prem).

The distillation workflow is more involved than LoRA
but well-supported by libraries like Hugging Face
`transformers`.

### Named techniques, distinguished

It is worth resisting the habit of calling all post-
training simply 'fine-tuning', since the term now covers
several techniques that differ in what they change, what
they cost, and what data they consume. We distinguish
five families.

**Instruction tuning** continues supervised training on
a corpus of instruction/response pairs so that the base
model follows instructions rather than merely continuing
text. It is what turns a raw pretrained model into a
usable assistant, and it operates on the full parameter
set. For a team using a frontier API this step is
already done; it becomes the team's concern only when
starting from a raw open-weights base.

**Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)** covers the
adapter family: Houlsby-style adapters
[@houlsby_2019_adapters], LoRA [@hu_2022_lora], and QLoRA
[@dettmers_2023_qlora]. These freeze the base and train a
small set of added parameters. They differ mainly in
where the added parameters sit and how the base is
stored: adapters insert new layers, LoRA adds low-rank
matrices to existing layers, and QLoRA does the same over
a 4-bit-quantized base so that training fits on a single
GPU.

**Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)**
trains a reward model on human preference comparisons and
then optimizes the policy against that reward; it is the
technique behind the aligned behavior of models such as
Llama 2 [@touvron_2023_llama2]. Constitutional AI
[@bai_2022_constitutional_ai] substitutes AI-generated
feedback against a written set of principles for much of
the human labeling. RLHF is effective but operationally
heavy: a separate reward model, an unstable optimization,
and substantial preference data.

**Direct preference optimization (DPO)** reaches a
similar objective to RLHF, making preferred outputs more
likely than dispreferred ones, without training a
separate reward model or running reinforcement learning;
it optimizes a preference loss directly. For teams that
want preference alignment but not the RLHF machinery, DPO
is the more tractable option.

**Continued pretraining** takes a general base and trains
it further on a large domain corpus so that it acquires
vocabulary and register the base lacks. This is how
models such as GatorTron [@yang_2022_gatortron] come to
read clinical text fluently. It is the most expensive
rung on the ladder and is rarely in scope for a team that
uses models rather than builds them.

For the great majority of research-analytics teams, none
of the preference-alignment or continued-pretraining
techniques is in scope; they are the province of groups
building models. We name them so that the vocabulary is
clear, since these terms are used loosely in practice and
the distinctions matter when reading a model card or a
methods section.

@tbl-customisation-methods sets the techniques side by
side. The reader may treat the final column as a rough
decision rule: the appropriate method is the cheapest one
whose 'when appropriate' condition matches the task.

| Method | Parameters trained | Data needed | Compute | When appropriate |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Prompting (zero/few-shot) | None | 0–20 examples | Inference only | Default; always try first |
| RAG | None | A corpus, not labels | Index + inference | Answer needs a specific corpus |
| Instruction tuning | All (~billions) | 10k–1M pairs | Multi-GPU | Starting from a raw base model |
| Adapters | ~0.5–5% | 1k–10k pairs | Single GPU | Behavior gap; modular per-task swapping |
| LoRA | ~0.1–1% | 1k–10k pairs | Single GPU | Behavior or style gap; standard PEFT |
| QLoRA | ~0.1–1% | 1k–10k pairs | Single modest GPU | LoRA when GPU memory is the binding limit |
| Full fine-tune | All (~billions) | 10k–100k+ pairs | Multi-GPU | PEFT insufficient and data plentiful |
| Continued pretraining | All (~billions) | Large domain corpus | Large cluster | Base lacks the domain's language |
| RLHF | Policy + reward model | 10k–100k preferences | Multi-GPU, unstable | Aligning behavior to preferences |
| DPO | All or a PEFT subset | 10k–100k preferences | One to a few GPUs | Preference alignment without the RL machinery |

: Customization and post-training techniques compared. The methods are ordered roughly by cost and by the labeled data they require. Prompting and RAG train no parameters at all and belong at the bottom of the ladder; the preference-alignment methods (RLHF, DPO) and continued pretraining sit at the top and are seldom in scope for teams that use rather than build models. {#tbl-customisation-methods}

The parameter-count column is the crux of the PEFT
argument. @fig-trainable-params makes it concrete: on a
log scale, the trainable-parameter counts span more than
three orders of magnitude, which is the whole reason PEFT
is attractive. LoRA and QLoRA move a few million
parameters where a full fine-tune moves billions, and
empirically reach comparable task performance
[@hu_2022_lora].

```{r}
#| label: fig-trainable-params
#| fig-cap: "Illustrative trainable-parameter counts for four customization methods applied to a seven-billion-parameter base model, on a log scale. LoRA and QLoRA train the same small set of parameters (QLoRA's saving is in memory, not in parameter count), a few million against the roughly seven billion of a full fine-tune. The gap of three to four orders of magnitude is why parameter-efficient methods dominate when a behavior gap must be closed on modest hardware. Counts are illustrative and vary with adapter rank, targeted modules, and base size."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
tp <- tibble::tribble(
  ~method,           ~params, ~kind,
  "LoRA (r = 8)",      4.2e6, "PEFT",
  "Adapters",         12.0e6, "PEFT",
  "LoRA (r = 64)",    34.0e6, "PEFT",
  "Full fine-tune",    7.0e9, "Full"
)
tp$method <- factor(tp$method, levels = tp$method[order(tp$params)])
fmt <- scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())
ggplot(tp, aes(method, params, fill = kind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt(params)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.4) +
  scale_y_log10(limits = c(1e6, 3e10), labels = fmt) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("PEFT" = "#1b6ca8", "Full" = "#b23a48")) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Trainable parameters (log scale)",
       fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

## Adoption in research-analytics teams

Mollick's *Cybernetic Teammate* RCT
[@mollick_2025_cybernetic_teammate] studied 776 professionals
at Procter & Gamble in a 4-arm trial: alone or in
two-person teams, with or without AI access, on
realistic product-development tasks. Findings:

- AI-enabled individuals matched the performance of
  two-person teams without AI (about a 0.37 SD
  improvement over baseline).
- AI-enabled teams outperformed non-AI teams,
  especially on the production of exceptional
  solutions.
- AI dissolved the expertise silo between R&D and
  commercial specialists; participants using AI
  reported higher positive emotion and lower
  anxiety.

We note that these are randomized results, which is still
uncommon in this literature and worth weighting
accordingly; the emerging body of RCT-style evidence on
human-AI teaming, of which this is a leading example, is
what lets us speak about effect sizes at all rather than
anecdote. On the other hand, the setting (product-
development tasks at a consumer-goods firm) is not health
research, so the magnitudes should be read as indicative
rather than directly transportable to a research-
analytics group.

The implications for a research-analytics team:

**Individual capability rises.** A researcher
working with AI assistance can produce work that
previously required the researcher plus a junior
researcher. The team's effective capacity increases by
some multiplier, the empirical estimates vary but are
substantial.

**Cross-discipline collaboration improves.** A
researcher collaborating with a clinician using
AI on both sides can communicate more efficiently;
the AI assists in translation across vocabularies.
Cross-discipline projects that previously had high
coordination cost become more tractable.

**The right unit is the augmented individual, not
the augmented team.** Many AI deployments default to
'the team uses AI' when the more productive pattern
is 'each person uses AI in their own work and shares
what works'. The team-level pattern emerges from the
individual-level adoption.

## Latent expertise: organizational R&D patterns

Mollick's *Latent Expertise* observation
[@mollick_2024_latent_expertise] is that the most useful AI
applications are discovered by individual
practitioners in their own work, not prescribed by
IT or product teams. The pattern that produces value
is:

1. Individuals experiment with AI in their work.
2. Useful patterns emerge.
3. Successful patterns are shared with peers.
4. Peers adapt and refine.
5. The team gradually codifies what works into
   conventions.
6. Codification feeds into onboarding for new
   team members.

This is recognizably a research-and-development
pattern, applied to AI workflow. It works because it
respects the diversity of work in the team, each
researcher's tasks are slightly different, and
allows local optimization.

The anti-pattern is centralized prescription: 'the
research-analytics team will use Tool X for Task Y, and
will use Prompt Z for Sub-task W'. This produces
compliance theater (people use the prescribed tool
when watched, and their own tools the rest of the
time) and misses the workflow innovations that come
from people who actually do the work.

The researcher (or team lead) supporting good
adoption:

- Encourages individual experimentation with AI
  tools.
- Sets up channels (Slack, internal Wiki, weekly
  show-and-tell) where people share what works.
- Captures successful patterns into shared
  conventions: a team prompt library, a team
  evaluation suite, a team's idiomatic API
  configuration.
- Onboards new team members into the conventions
  rather than into individual tools.
- Periodically refreshes the conventions as new
  patterns emerge.

A specific working pattern for a 6–10 person
research-analytics group:

- A shared `prompts/` directory in the team's
  internal repo, with per-task prompt templates.
- A `runbooks/` directory with specific workflows
  (e.g., 'how we do RoB assessment with LLM
  assistance').
- A weekly 30-minute show-and-tell where one
  person demonstrates a recent AI workflow that
  worked well.
- A monthly update to the team's evaluation suite
  based on lessons learned.

## Worked example: a research-analytics team's first 6 months

A research-analytics group of 7 people adopts AI
assistance starting Q1 2026. The trajectory:

**Month 1: individual experimentation.** Each team
member is given a frontier API budget (~$50/month)
and encouraged to try AI assistance on routine work.
A weekly meeting captures observations, frustrations,
discoveries.

**Month 2: emerging patterns.** Three patterns have
clear value: (1) boilerplate code generation, (2)
methods-section drafting, (3) literature scoping.
The team agrees informal conventions: AI-drafted
methods sections are reviewed by another team member
before submission, AI-generated code is run with
test data before commitment.

**Month 3: codification.** The team builds a shared
prompt library for the three patterns. The library
includes example outputs and the verification regime
expected for each. Each team member contributes their
working prompts.

**Month 4: evaluation.** The team builds an
evaluation suite (per @sec-evaluation) with 25 tasks
reflecting their actual work. They evaluate the
frontier API on the suite as a baseline; they will
re-run the evaluation when models update.

**Month 5: workflow integration.** The patterns are
integrated into the team's standard workflows.
Methods-drafting templates link to the methods-
drafting prompts. The team's analytical SOPs include
verification steps that explicitly cover AI-generated
artifacts. Onboarding for a new junior researcher
includes the conventions.

**Month 6: customization question.** The team
considers fine-tuning. Looking at the data, the only
task where context engineering consistently
underperforms is generating SAS code in the
institution's house style (deep PROC SQL nesting,
specific macro libraries). They build a 200-example
library, set up retrieval over it, and find the
results match their target. They decide against
fine-tuning at this stage; the example-library
approach works.

**6-month retrospective.** The team's effective
capacity has increased materially (rough estimate:
30–40% more analytical output for the same headcount).
Junior researchers are productive on tasks that
previously required senior involvement. The team's
analytical reports are more thoroughly prepared
because the AI-assisted drafting frees time for
review. No clinical errors attributable to AI
assistance have been reported; verification has
caught all material errors before they reached
publication.

The pattern is reproducible: encourage experimentation,
share what works, codify patterns, and defer
customization until clearly necessary.

## Collaborating with an LLM on customization and team adoption

Three prompt patterns illustrate working with LLMs on
adoption-shaped problems.

**Prompt 1: 'Should we fine-tune for this task?'**
Provide the task description and the current
context-engineering performance.

*What to watch for.* The LLM tends to recommend
fine-tuning when context engineering would suffice.
Push back: 'what would have to be true for context
engineering to fail here? have we tested those
conditions?'

*Verification.* The decision is empirical. Run the
context-engineering version against the evaluation
suite; if it scores below the team's threshold,
investigate why. Often the failure is improvable
without fine-tuning.

**Prompt 2: 'Help our team adopt AI for analytic
work.'** Provide the team's structure and current
processes.

*What to watch for.* The LLM tends to recommend
top-down rollouts: 'choose a tool, train the team,
mandate use'. The Mollick evidence suggests
bottom-up adoption is more effective. Push toward
patterns that respect individual variation.

*Verification.* Read the LLM's recommendations
against the *Cybernetic Teammate* and *Latent
Expertise* findings. If the recommendations are
top-down-prescriptive, modify them.

**Prompt 3: 'Build a prompt library for our team.'**
Provide a list of the team's tasks.

*What to watch for.* The LLM produces a competent
draft library. The library is a starting point; the
team owns it and refines it. Do not adopt the
LLM's prompts wholesale without team review.

*Verification.* Each prompt in the library is
tested against representative tasks before adoption.
The team's evaluation suite is the criterion.

The meta-pattern: **adoption is a team practice, not
a tool-purchase decision.** The LLM accelerates
the construction of artifacts (prompt libraries,
runbooks, evaluation suites) but the team's
disposition and discipline are what make them work.

## Principle in use

Three habits define defensible work in this area:

1. **Default to context engineering.** Fine-tuning is
   expensive and obsoletes; context engineering is
   cheap and survives base-model updates.
   Customisation is for when context demonstrably
   fails.

2. **Encourage individual discovery.** Adoption
   emerges at the team-member level. The team
   lead's job is to surface and codify patterns,
   not to prescribe them.

3. **Treat conventions as living.** The team's
   prompt library, evaluation suite, and runbooks
   are living artifacts updated as patterns evolve.
   A frozen library decays.

## Exercises

1. Catalog your team's routine tasks. For each,
   identify whether context engineering, fine-tuning,
   or distillation is the right starting point.

2. Build a prompt library entry for one of your
   team's most common tasks. Include the prompt,
   example inputs, expected outputs, and verification
   steps.

3. Run a 4-week experiment in your team: each
   member tracks one AI-assisted task per week.
   Aggregate the patterns at the end of the month.

4. Calculate the cost of a LoRA fine-tune for a
   task you would consider customizing. Include
   compute, training data construction, and
   maintenance over a year. Compare to context
   engineering.

5. Audit your team's current AI adoption. Identify
   one centralized prescription and one bottom-up
   pattern. Reflect on which is producing more value.

## Further reading

- @hu_2022_lora, *LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large
  Language Models*. The reference paper for the
  LoRA method.
- @dettmers_2023_qlora, *QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning
  of Quantized LLMs*. The reference for the
  quantization-plus-LoRA approach that makes
  fine-tuning practically accessible.
- @houlsby_2019_adapters, *Parameter-Efficient
  Transfer Learning for NLP*. The earlier
  adapter-based PEFT paper that informs the LoRA
  family.
- @bolton_2024_biomedlm, *BioMedLM*. The
  open-weights biomedical language model that is
  the natural starting point for biomedical
  on-prem deployment.
- @yang_2022_gatortron, *GatorTron*. A clinical
  language model produced by continued pretraining
  on a large corpus of electronic-health-record
  text; illustrates the top rung of the ladder.
- @touvron_2023_llama2, *Llama 2*. Documents an
  open-weights model whose aligned behavior comes
  from an RLHF pipeline.
- @bai_2022_constitutional_ai, *Constitutional AI*.
  Replaces much of the human preference labeling in
  RLHF with AI feedback against written principles.
- @mollick_2025_cybernetic_teammate, *The Cybernetic
  Teammate*. The RCT evidence underwriting the
  augmented-individual framing.
- @mollick_2024_latent_expertise, *Latent Expertise: Everyone
  is in R&D*. The argument for bottom-up adoption.
